<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and clashed cleanly on the same axis: whether a five-year deadline plus targeted cash is a better protection technology than a universal price floor. PRO built a coherent fairness-and-leakage case (assistance proportional to litres consumed is indefensible; an endpoint prevents "temporary" subsidies becoming permanent) and made an honest, useful concession that exclusion is a serious cost. But CON located and exploited the sharper asymmetry: the deadline binds the executable half of the reform (raising pump prices) while the protective half (enrolled, indexed, delivered payments) remains discretionary. CON's pressure questions were the pivot of the debate: Q1 forced PRO to offer "legal indexation entitlement," and Q2 extracted the explicit admission that subsidies should end by year five even if millions of displaced and undocumented households remain unpaid. CON then converted that into the strongest weighing move of the debate — every PRO safeguard presupposes exactly the state capacity whose absence justifies the concern, so a competent state needs no calendar and an incompetent one merely schedules the harm. CON also blunted PRO's fairness engine by conceding the regressive tail (tiered/lifeline pricing, ending industrial concessions), which captured much of PRO's moral appeal while preserving the price floor, and answered PRO's "indefinite postponement" question with a concrete auditable trigger plus conditionality. PRO's best counters — that subsidised fuel also does not guarantee delivery, and that CON demands verified delivery from cash while tolerating unverified delivery through fuel — were genuinely good and kept the debate competitive, but they were partly answered by CON's "fuel is an input" point (diesel prices move bread, fares and irrigation, so the price floor reaches the poor indirectly and immediately, whereas transfers lag). CON's two clipped turns are a real execution cost and trim the margin, but the decisive comparison still resolves in CON's favour.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q2 and the follow-through: forcing PRO to state that universal subsidies should end at year five even with millions still outside payments, then framing it as "the calendar binds the easy variable and leaves the protective one on a promise," with the paradox that PRO's safeguards (legal monthly indexation, displacement-based enrollment) require the very capacity whose absence is the problem. PRO's reply — that subsidies do not guarantee delivery either — mitigated but did not neutralise it.</best_rebuttal>
